name: Niuafo'ou
confidence_why: Tsukamoto (1988), a full grammar from fieldwork, states and exemplifies primary stress fixed on the second-to-last vowel of the word with long vowels counting as two, and the only other description, Collocott's brief 1922 note that Niuafo'ouans 'raise the voice on final words and syllables', describes sentence cadence rather than word stress and its one marked example, fale néi, itself follows the penultimate rule.
catalog_citation: Tsukamoto, Akihisa. 1988. The language of Niuafo'ou Island. PhD thesis, Australian National University, Canberra. xiii+482 pp.
catalog_locator: Part I ch. 3 'Stress', §3.1 and §3.1.1 (A) 'Demarcative Stress in Simple Words', p. 43; §1.4 'The Structure of the Syllable', p. 30; §3.2 'Stress Shifting - Definitive Stress', p. 52 and p. 56; secondary-stress restrictions and clitics p. 44; affixes, reduplication, compounds pp. 45-49; fast speech §3.1.2 pp. 49-52; emphatic stress §3.3 pp. 56-58.
catalog_quote: [p. 43] Simple words constitute phonological words by themselves. Primary stress, [ˊ], occurs fixedly on the second-to-last vowel of the word, and the secondary stress, [ˋ], as a basic rule, every other preceding vowel. poo [pó:] 'night' tai [tá·i] 'sea' pato [pá·to] 'duck' kofi [kó·fi] 'coffee' kulii [kulí:] 'dog' hoosi [hoó·si] or [hoó·ʃi] 'horse' paito [paí·to] 'kitchen' fafine [fafí·ne] 'woman' letioo [lètió:] 'radio' ngaaue [ŋà:ú·e] 'work' [p. 30] The sequences of the same vowels, however, function exactly in the same way as any sequence of two CV's in other respects such as the placement of primary stress (I.3.1.1-2.) or the form of reduplication (I.2.2.3.). Therefore, all the (C)VV sequences are regarded as consisting of two syllables. [p. 52] In Niuafo'ou, as in Tongan, the definiteness of nominal phrases is indicated by stress shift. ... the shifting of stress takes place in the last word of a phrase, namely, in the word just preceding the expected deictic. It affects not only the primary stress but also the preceding secondary stresses, if any, but its effect does not extend across a phonological word boundary. ... poo [pó:] 'night' poó [poó·] '(the) night (definite)' fale [fá·le] 'house' falé [falé·] '(the) house (definite)'
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Demarcative stress occurs in a fixed position of certain segments in the stream of speech and marks their boundaries. Segments that are thus indicated differ somewhat from words as defined in II.1.2. and will be referred to as phonological words. [...] Simple words constitute phonological words by themselves. Primary stress, [ˊ], occurs fixedly on the second-to-last vowel of the word, and the secondary stress, [ˋ], as a basic rule, every other preceding vowel.
new_statements.citation: Tsukamoto, Akihisa. 1988. The language of Niuafo'ou Island. PhD thesis, Australian National University, Canberra. Part I, ch. 3 'Stress', §3.1.1 (A) 'Demarcative Stress in Simple Words'.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: copies we hold opened: (496 pp, image-only, 81,719,634 bytes; the PDF's metadata: Canon scan, A4). I rendered p. 57 (= thesis p. 43, offset +14 confirmed by the printed folio '43' on the page) at 110 dpi and read the page scan directly, not the scanned. The quoted passage is there verbatim: 'CHAPTER 3 / Stress / 3.1 Demarcative Stress / Demarcative stress occurs in a fixed position of certain segments in the stream of speech and marks their boundaries. Segments that are thus indicated differ somewhat from words as defined in II.1.2. and will be referred to as phonological words..' and under '3.1.1 Demarcative Stress in Slow Speech, (A) Demarcative Stress in Simple Words': 'Simple words cons…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate vowel of the phonological word, counting each vowel/mora separately (long vowels count as two: poo [pó:] 'night', kulii [kulí:] 'dog', letioo [lètió:] 'radio'), so it is a penultimate-mora rule of the Tongan type; secondary stress on alternating preceding vowels (pàsikàla, sìokàalafi). Monosyllabic words and monosyllabic affixes never form phonological words on their own but cliticise to a neighbour, so the deictics ni/na, the person determiners ke/ne, the articles te/he and monosyllabic suffixes pull the primary stress one vowel to the right (fale [fále] but fale ni [falé-ni]); bisyllabic affixes carry their own stress. In nominal phrases, definiteness is marked by shifting the primary (and preceding secondary) stress to the last vowel of the phrase-final word ('definitive stress', §3.2, pp. 52-56).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: 'as a basic rule, every other preceding vowel' (p. 43); it never falls on the second vowel of two identical vowels or of a rising vowel sequence, or on inserted /i/ in loans, in which case it skips to the preceding vowel (p. 44); in fast speech non-phrase-final primary stresses reduce to secondary with a tendency to alternate stronger and weaker stresses (pp. 49-52).
new_statements.exceptions: Definitive stress: phrase-final word of a definite nominal phrase takes stress on its final vowel (fale 'house' vs falé '(the) house', tangata vs tangatá), with the exceptional placement on the emphatic possessive determiner (ta'akú kulii) (pp. 52-56); monosyllabic clitics (deictics ni/na, determiners ke/ne, articles te/he, monosyllabic suffixes) shift stress rightwards (pp. 44-47); reduplicated syllables of Type II are unstressed (p. 48); emphatic (contrastive and intensity) stress with vowel protraction (pp. 56-58).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the 'phonological word' (slow-speech citation forms), explicitly distinguished from the grammatical word: monosyllables and monosyllabic affixes cliticise, bisyllabic affixes and each member of compounds/base-modifier sequences form their own phonological word; the fixed rule is stated for slow speech, with reduction in fast speech described separately; definitive stress is a phrase-level shift.
new_statements.identity_note: Tsukamoto 1988 describes Niuafo'ou (niua1240) as spoken on Niuafo'ou Island and by resettled speakers, based on deliberate speech of informants who consciously avoided Tongan forms (thesis p. 9); he notes heavy Tongan influence in spontaneous speech. No dialect split is described; the stress system is the same type as Tongan (tong1325) including the definitive-stress shift.

new_statements.quote: ACCENTUATION. The general effect of the speech of Niua Fo'ou on the ear is different from that of Tongan. The Niua Fo'ouans raise the voice on final words and syllables, giving the language a cadence not unlike that of Samoan. [...] Connected with the accentuation of final syllables in Niua Fo'ou, whereas the accent in Tongan normally falls on the penultimate, is the fuller form in Niua Fo'ou of nei , this, which in Tongan has become an enclitic ni . Tongan, ko e falé ni ( ni enclitic), N.F. ko te fale néi , this house.
new_statements.citation: Collocott, E. E. V. 1922. The speech of Niua Fo'ou. Journal of the Polynesian Society 31(4): 185-189.
new_statements.locator: p. 188, paragraph headed 'ACCENTUATION' (within the 'PHONOLOGY' part of the article)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (page markers 185-189 all present) and re-downloaded the same Internet Archive copy (20180209140917) into the 26,553 bytes, same size as the copy consulted, same text. The ACCENTUATION paragraph is on p. 188 inside the PHONOLOGY part, immediately after the GLOTTAL STOP paragraph; both quoted sentences ('The Niua Fo'ouans raise the voice on final words and syllables, giving the language a cadence not unlike that of Samoan.' and 'Connected with the accentuation of final syllables in Niua Fo'ou, whereas the accent in Tongan normally falls on the penultimate, is the fuller form in Niua Fo'ou of nei, this, which in Tongan has become an enclitic ni. Tongan, ko e fale ni (ni enclitic), N.F.…
new_statements.relation_note: Taken literally ('accentuation of final syllables' vs Tongan penultimate) it differs from the catalog's Tsukamoto 1988 rule (primary stress fixedly on the second-to-last vowel, i.e. penultimate mora, with definitive stress shifting to the last syllable only in definite phrase-final words). But the observation is about phrase-final voice raising ('cadence'), not a word-stress rule, and Collocott's own example fale néi is consistent with penultimate-vowel stress; it most plausibly records phrase-final intonation and/or Tsukamoto's definitive stress rather than a different word-stress system. Not weighty enough to overturn the catalog record.
new_statements.rule_in_words: An impressionistic 1922 observation: speakers 'raise the voice on final words and syllables', giving a sentence cadence like Samoan (he cites Tregear & Smith 1907 on sentence-final emphasis in Niuean), and he speaks of 'the accentuation of final syllables in Niua Fo'ou' as opposed to the Tongan penultimate accent. No word-level rule is stated and no stress-marked wordlist is given; the single marked example, fale néi 'this house', puts the accent on the second-to-last vowel of the phrase-final word nei (n-e-i), which is what a penultimate-vowel rule predicts, so the 'final' claim rests on sentence-final pitch raising rather than on word stress. No secondary stress, no weight, no exceptions.
new_statements.exceptions: none; contrasts Tongan enclitic ni (falé ni) with the full Niuafo'ou form nei (fale néi)
new_statements.identity_note: All three sources describe the Niuafo'ou language of Niuafo'ou Island itself (Collocott from a short visit in c. 1921, noting the dialect was already being displaced by Tongan; Dye from fieldwork Dec 1976-Jan 1977, noting the population's 1946-c.1960 relocation to 'Eua; Tsukamoto 1988 ANU thesis). Collocott explicitly contrasts it with Tongan and with Niuatoputapu (which he says shows 'practically no variations from ordinary Tongan'). No sub-dialect is named in any source.

readall_conflicts: Collocott 1922 (p. 188) says Niuafo'ouans 'raise the voice on final words and syllables' and speaks of 'the accentuation of final syllables in Niua Fo'ou, whereas the accent in Tongan normally falls on the penultimate'; the catalog's source Tsukamoto 1988 (ch. 3, thesis p. 43) states that primary stress 'occurs fixedly on the second-to-last vowel of the word' (penultimate mora; long vowels count as two vowels) with secondary stress on every other preceding vowel and a separate 'definitive stress' on the last syllable of definite phrase-final words. The two disagree on the surface (final vs penultimate), but Collocott's remark is an impressionistic description of sentence cadence with no word-stress data, and his only marked example (fale néi) matches Tsukamoto's rule, so the disagreement is resolved in favour of Tsukamoto: Collocott most likely heard phrase-final intonation and/or definitive stress. Dye 1980 is silent on stress.

tone.quote: また、ニウアフォッオウ語でもトンガ語でも（また、ウヴェア語でも）名詞句の決定詞 ― 英語の冠詞・所有代名詞に相当する語 ― が特定・非特定（話し手にとって既知か未知か）の区別を示し、強勢が語末から二番目の音節にあるか、語末の音節にあるかによって定・不定（聞き手にとって既知か未知か）の区別を示す。
tone.translation: Moreover, in Niuafo'ou as in Tongan (and also in Uvean) the determiner of the noun phrase — the word corresponding to the English article or possessive pronoun — marks the specific/non-specific distinction (known or unknown to the speaker), and whether the stress lies on the second syllable from the end of the word or on the final syllable marks the definite/indefinite distinction (known or unknown to the hearer).
